---
layout: post
title: Flashing OpenWrt onto a Cudy WR3000P Wi-Fi router
categories: [OpenWrt,U-Boot]
---

The Cudy WR3000P is a Wi-Fi 6 router that has excellent support by the OpenWrt
project. It has a MediaTek MT7981 (Filogic 820) 64-bit dual-core 1.3 GHz CPU,
512MB of DDR4 RAM, a 2.5Gb WAN port, 4x1 Gb Lan ports, and can be powered by PoE
via the WAN port.

Full technical details for the router can be found on [the OpenWrt project’s device page for the Cudy WR3000P v1](https://openwrt.org/toh/cudy/wr3000p_v1).

![](/images/{{ page.id }}/cudy-wr3000p.jpg)

There are two OpenWrt builds for the Cudy WR3000P: a standard build which can be
flashed using the stock OEM firmware onto the existing UBI partition, and which
works with the stock flash partition layout. This is by far the easiest and
safest way to flash OpenWrt on the WR3000P.

There is also a second "ubootmod" build, which includes a new U-Boot bootloader
and a modified partition layout. This is considerably more work to do, and
carries more risk of bricking the router, but has some benefits.

Both procedures are documented here.

# Flashing OpenWrt using the OEM firmware

For the steps documented here, I followed [the OpenWrt project’s device page for the Cudy WR3000P v1](https://openwrt.org/toh/cudy/wr3000p_v1).

## Download the intermediate OpenWrt image from the Cudy website

The intermediate image is needed because the stock Cudy firmware will only allow flashing the device with images that have been cryptographically signed by Cudy, which the standard openwrt images have not. Once the device has been flashed with the intermediate firmware, we can then use it to flash whatever version of openwrt we like.

Download the intermediate firmware image from [the Cudy website](https://www.cudy.com/en-us/blogs/faq/openwrt-software-download). Note the warnings about a recent change to the flash chip in 3000 series devices since November 2025, which won’t boot openwrt images older than the 24.10.5 release. If you are using this version or newer, you can ignore this as they fully support the newer flash chip. The Cudy page above explains how to check which version device you have if you are concerned about it.

Download the '[WR3000P 1.0.zip'](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_Om5G9Audep1TfSTSwmB4j7FLI6ZVYqa/view?usp=drive_link) file (or newer) from [the google drive folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1BKVarlwlNxf7uJUtRhuMGUqeCa5KpMnj).

Unzip this file to unpack the image, which will be called something like `cudy_wr3000p-v1-sysupgrade_20251119.bin`.

## Download an OpenWrt image from the OpenWrt project

You need the latest sysupgrade image for the `cudy_wr3000p-v1` build target. Remember that if you have a model that has the newer flash chip in it, you need version 24.10.5 or above. The easiest way to find an image is by using [the OpenWrt Firmware Selector](https://firmware-selector.openwrt.org/?version=25.12.6&target=mediatek%2Ffilogic&id=cudy_wr3000p-v1).

I downloaded [this image](https://downloads.openwrt.org/releases/25.12.5/targets/mediatek/filogic/openwrt-25.12.5-mediatek-filogic-cudy_wr3000p-v1-squashfs-sysupgrade.bin).

## Power up the router

Connect an ethernet cable to the router’s WAN port. I used an appropriate VLAN on my home network.

Connect up the power via the barrel jack adaptor. This router is also capable of being powered via PoE on the WAN port, but I haven’t tried that yet.

You should now be able to connect to the Cudy’s Wifi access point, which will be called something like “Cudy-XXXX”. The Wifi password is printed on the bottom of the router.

You can now open the Cudy’s web portal in a browser at `http://192.168.10.1`.

When you first access the portal, it will ask you to set an admin user password. This will only be temporary as you’ll be flashing the firmware with openwrt and that will have a different admin user and password.

Go through the rest of the setup wizard, accepting the defaults.

![][image1]

## Flash the device with the intermediate image

Browse to “General Settings” and then “Firmware”.

Under the “Local Update” section, click “Browse” and select the `cudy_wr3000p-v1-sysupgrade_20251119.bin` intermediate image from the “WR3000P 1.0.zip” file. Click Proceed when ready.

![][image3]

Note, the above step failed with an image verification error. I had to go to “Advanced Settings” and then “Firmware” and select the image from there, which worked.

After a few minutes the router should tell you it is rebooting.

## Flash the sysupgrade image

The intermediate image is OpenWrt, so its luci web interface is available on [http\://192.168.1.1](http://192.168.1.1). Note for me the intermediate image came up with no Wi-fi enabled, so I had to connect to it via a network cable connected to one of the Lan ports on the router.

Browse to “System” \-\> “Backup / Flash Firmware”. Under “Flash new firmware image” select the sysupgrade image you downloaded from the openwrt website (not the Cudy one\!).

Deselect the “Keep settings” option because you don’t have any settings worth saving at this point and you want the settings from the latest image.

Click “Continue”.

![][image4]

![][image5]

When it has finished flashing the router will reboot, and OpenWrt will be ready
for you to configure as you wish.

# Recovering from a broken install

It's possible to recover from a non-bootable firmware install by pressing and holding down the reset button while powering on the router, which will put the device into a recovery mode, where it will attemp to pull a recovery image using TFTP. It assumes a TFTP server on 192.168.1.88. However, unfortunately the stock bootloader will only boot images signed by Cudy, so will only boot the official OEM firmware images and not the openwrt initramfs images. However, you can recover an openwrt system by reinstalling the stock OEM firmware via this method, and then follow the above steps to reinstall openwrt.

The steps for this recovery method are documented on [the Cudy website](https://www.cudy.com/en-gb/blogs/faq/how-to-recovery-the-cudy-router-from-openwrt-firmware-to-cudy-official-firmware).

If you want a bootloader that will allow you to boot openwrt initramfs rescue images, you can flash the bootloader with the mainline U-Boot bootloader, which is supported for the Cudy WR300P since openwrt 25.12. The steps to do this are documented below. Replacing the bootloader involves a risk of bricking your router, so you do so at your own risk.

# Backup OEM partitions

The partition table on the flash drive can be seen by SSHing to the router when running openwrt:

```shell
cat /proc/mtd
dev:    size   erasesize  name
mtd0: 00100000 00020000 "BL2"
mtd1: 00080000 00020000 "u-boot-env"
mtd2: 00200000 00020000 "Factory"
mtd3: 00040000 00020000 "bdinfo"
mtd4: 00200000 00020000 "FIP"
mtd5: 04000000 00020000 "ubi"
```

The “ubi” partition is where firmware including openwrt lives, including the overlay filesystem. “BL2” is the preboot first stage bootloader. “FIP” is the main bootloader. “Factory” holds wifi radio calibration data, and “bdinfo” contains board info and MAC addresses. You will need all of these if you ever want to recover the system if the flash becomes corrupted, or to restore the OEM firmware. In particular, the Factory and bdinfo partitions hold data which are specific to your device and can’t be recovered by other means. So you should take a backup of all these partitions. You don’t need a backup of the “ubi” partition as this is the firmware partition and can be restored using the steps above.

```shell
ssh root@192.168.1.1
dd if=/dev/mtd0 of=/tmp/BL2.bin
dd if=/dev/mtd1 of=/tmp/u-boot-env.bin
dd if=/dev/mtd2 of=/tmp/Factory.bin
dd if=/dev/mtd3 of=/tmp/bdinfo.bin
dd if=/dev/mtd4 of=/tmp/FIP.bin
apk add openssh-sftp-server
```

Now use the `scp` command to copy these off the router onto your client device and store them somewhere safe, such as google drive or a NAS server.

# Flashing the U-Boot bootloader onto the Cudy WR3000P V1 (ubootmod)

The stock bootloader on the Cudy WR3000 series routers is a modified version of U-Boot. It supports rescuing the system by pulling an image with TFTP, but will only accept images that have been signed by Cudy, which means either the stock firmware or the transition openwrt image. It won’t boot openwrt initramfs rescue images, which makes it more difficult to recover a bricked router.

Also, for some reason, the stock partition layout on the WR3000 series routers does not make use of all 128MB of the flash drive. When flashed with OpenWrt, only 44MB is available to use for packages and configuration.

Fortunately, since the release of version 25.12, OpenWrt now supports a modified flash partition layout by replacing the stock bootloader with a mainline U-Boot bootloader, which is known as the “ubootmod”. The benefits of doing this are:

1. Unlocks the free space of the flash chip, making \~95MB available to the firmware versus 44MB with the stock layout
2. Makes it easier to recover from bad firmware by allowing booting from any image of your choice including mainline openwrt
3. Gives you a proper open source bootloader, replacing the modified Cudy one

__Warning\! There is a significant risk of bricking your router if the process goes wrong.__ If the BL2 or FIP partitions are broken, you will need to dismantle the router and flash a bootloader using the serial pads on the PCB. This guide doesn’t cover how to do that, but you can follow the install steps on [the T-56 device page](https://openwrt.org/toh/zyxel/t-56#installation) which documents a similar process.

## Backup OEM partitions

The ubootmod install process changes the partition layout on the WR3000P, which
will overwrite the OEM partitions and the data they contain, so it is very
important that you backup these partitions before you proceed with the ubootmod
process. If you haven't done so already, follow the steps in the "Backup OEM
partitions" section above before continuing.

You will also need to SSH in to the router and run commands in a shell, so you
will need to flash it with a version of OpenWrt, for example the intermediate
openwrt image. If you've not done so already, follow the steps above to flash
the intermediate openwrt image onto the router.

## Prep a TFTP server with a rescue image

On your client device, install a TFTP server. I use Linux, so the instructions here are Linux specific, but if you’re using Windows there are instructions on how to do this [here](https://www.cudy.com/en-gb/blogs/faq/how-to-recovery-the-cudy-router-from-openwrt-firmware-to-cudy-official-firmware).

Install the tftps-hpa package:

```shell
sudo apt install tftpd-hpa
```

The default config should be fine. It will serve files from the `/src/tftp` directory.

Download an OpenWrt initramfs rescue image. Note, you’ll need the ubootmod one because the partition table will have been modified when it boots:

```shell
wget https://downloads.openwrt.org/releases/25.12.6/targets/mediatek/filogic/openwrt-25.12.6-mediatek-filogic-cudy_wr3000p-v1-ubootmod-initramfs-recovery.itb
```

Copy it to the /src/tftp directory, renaming it like so:

```shell
sudo cp -p Downloads/openwrt-25.12.6-mediatek-filogic-cudy_wr3000p-v1-initramfs-kernel.bin /srv/tftp/openwrt-mediatek-filogic-cudy_wr3000p-v1-ubootmod-initramfs-recovery.itb
```

Make sure your client device is allowing connections to the TFTP port 69\. I had to stop my firewall temporarily.

Test it from your router:

```shell
ssh root@192.168.1.1
apk update
apk add atftp
atftp
tftp> connect 192.168.1.XXX
tftp> get openwrt-mediatek-filogic-cudy_wr3000p-v1-ubootmod-initramfs-recovery.itb
tftp> quit
```

Replace `XXX` with the last octet of your client device’s IP address. You should have the above file on the router. If not, it didn't work.

## Download the new bootloader images

On the router, SSH in and do the following:

```shell
ssh root@192.168.1.1
apk add curl
curl -L https://downloads.openwrt.org/releases/25.12.6/targets/mediatek/filogic/openwrt-25.12.6-mediatek-filogic-cudy_wr3000p-v1-ubootmod-preloader.bin > /tmp/bl2.bin
curl -L https://downloads.openwrt.org/releases/25.12.6/targets/mediatek/filogic/openwrt-25.12.6-mediatek-filogic-cudy_wr3000p-v1-ubootmod-bl31-uboot.fip > /tmp/uboot.fip
```

Verify the image files are valid by comparing the SHA256 hashes against the [openwrt download page](https://firmware-selector.openwrt.org/?version=25.12.6&target=mediatek%2Ffilogic&id=cudy_wr3000p-v1-ubootmod):

```shell
sha256sum /tmp/uboot.fip /tmp/bl2.bin
b35a8b367315d7db78c948234a8f71a17f9486d68814d200b3b893726a59976d  /tmp/uboot.fip
9be2b11ca74912f29ef984e33b8ced740a9bdb02411ba9dcb9b464bcf53e5442  /tmp/bl2.bin
```

## Flash the bootloader images

Tell openwrt to allow writing to the bootloader partitions. This is blocked by default. Load the mtd-rw module with the “i\_want\_a\_brick” flag to allow writes to the bootloader partitions.

```shell
apk add kmod-mtd-rw
insmod mtd-rw i_want_a_brick=1
```

Now flash the BL2 and FIP partitions:

```shell
mtd write /tmp/bl2.bin BL2
mtd write /tmp/uboot.fip FIP
```

Now disconnect the network cable from the Lan port and add the IP address `192.168.1.254` to your client device on the interface that will be connected to the router.

```shell
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.254/24 dev enp0s31f6
```

Now power off the router, connect the network cable and power the router back on. After a minute or so you should see the LEDs on the router flash rapidly and then settle. You should then be able to SSH into the rescue system:

```shell
ssh root@192.168.1.1
```

## Reformat the mtd5 (ubi) partition to make use of all the available space

```shell
ubidetach -p /dev/mtd5
ubiformat -y /dev/mtd5
ubiattach -p /dev/mtd5
ubimkvol /dev/ubi0 -n 0 -N ubootenv -s 128KiB
ubimkvol /dev/ubi0 -n 1 -N ubootenv2 -s 128KiB
```

## Flash a sysupgrade image onto the uci partition

Grab the sysupgrade image on your client device, remembering to use the ubootmod one:

```shell
wget https://downloads.openwrt.org/releases/25.12.6/targets/mediatek/filogic/openwrt-25.12.6-mediatek-filogic-cudy_wr3000p-v1-ubootmod-squashfs-sysupgrade.itb
```

Now in your browser, open [http\://192.168.1.1/](http://192.168.1.1/). You should see the OpenWrt Luci login page. Click the Login button (there’s no password yet) and go to System \-\> Backup / Flash Firmware, then under the “Flash new firmware image” section, select the sysupgrade image you downloaded above, and flash it. Do not keep the settings as there aren’t any yet.

![][image6]

After a minute or so, the router will reboot and you will see the login screen for your new OpenWrt system with the ubootmod partition layout.

## Restoring the OEM partition layout and firmware

I haven’t tried this myself, but in theory you can flash the BL2 and FIP partitions from the backups you took earlier, then follow [Cudy’s recovery guide to install the OEM firmware](https://www.cudy.com/en-gb/blogs/faq/how-to-recovery-the-cudy-router-from-openwrt-firmware-to-cudy-official-firmware).

The steps to do this are documented [here](https://4pda.to/forum/index.php?showtopic=1087457&st=6040#entry142244794).
